Verdict — the answer is “optimise the tests”, twice over

1. forkCount works, and it is blocked by a test bug, not by hardware. Measured back-to-back on the loom subtree: 8m 01s → 3m 09s at forkCount=4, a 2.5× speed-up for +1.7 GB of RAM. But failures went from 10 to 233 out of the same 1,830 tests: every test JVM shares one target/test-config directory and races on the JWT keystore inside it. The test code already carries the TODO. Fix that and the 2.5× is available; ship it without fixing that and the suite lies to you.

2. One test class is 58% of the whole suite, and no fork count can touch it. WhisperNodeTest spends 15m 04s running real speech-to-text inference inside mvn test. A class runs in one fork, so this is a hard floor on the 25m 55s total. Moving it to failsafe takes the suite to 10m 10s on its own — a bigger win than any forkCount change, at no risk.

3. forkCount can never be raised globally as things stand. cortex/** inherits no -Xmx, so one scene-detection fork already peaks at 27.8 GB and a captioning fork at 18.3 GB. Two of those at once do not fit in 62 GB — a whole-reactor attempt at forkCount=4 aborted with a fork that could not start.

Two numbers frame everything below.

The suite is almost entirely test execution. 99% of wall clock is inside test JVMs; Maven's own resolution, compile and plugin work is 15.9s. (This was a warm incremental build — a clean build adds compile time that forkCount cannot touch.)

The machine is almost idle while it runs. Test JVMs consumed 88m 06s of CPU time across 25m 39s of wall time — an average of 3.4 busy cores out of 24. There is real headroom. The rest of this report is about how much of it is actually reachable.

2. Two surefire regimes

The reactor is not configured uniformly, and the difference decides where forkCount can go.

RegimeApplies toModulesClasses ForksHeap capDeclared in
Fresh JVM per test class
reuseForks=false, forkCount=1		 loom/**
loom-shared/**		 19238 238 -Xmx256m loom/pom.xml
loom-shared/pom.xml
One reused JVM per module
surefire defaults		 cortex/**, cli,
loom-client/**, integration-test		 51264 51 none root pom.xml
(plugin declared, no config)
  • loom/** pays a JVM start for every test class — 238 starts costing about 2m 00s in total. It is heap-capped, so it is the safe place to add forks.
  • cortex/** starts one JVM per module (cheap) but has no heap ceiling, which is exactly what makes a global fork increase dangerous — see §5.

loom/pom.xml already parameterises this as <forkCount>${surefire.forkcount}</forkCount>, so -Dsurefire.forkcount=N works today with no pom change. The root/cortex configuration has no such property.

5. Memory — the real fork ceiling

Worst peak resident set reached by any single test JVM in each module, from the kernel's own high-water mark (ru_maxrss). This is the number forkCount multiplies:

Median fork 278 MB; 90th percentile 431 MB; worst 27.8 GB. The distribution is not merely skewed — the top entry is 66× the 90th percentile.

Root cause cortex forks have no heap ceiling

The root pom.xml declares maven-surefire-plugin with no <configuration>, so cortex forks take the JVM default max heap — about 15 GB on this 62 GB host, before native OpenCV/FFmpeg buffers are added on top. The loom/** forks are capped at -Xmx256m and behave: none exceeds 502 MB.

Consequence: forkCount=2 applied globally would ask for roughly 56 GB in scene-detection alone — an OOM kill, not a speed-up. Fix this before touching forkCount globally. It is also a latent hazard today for anyone running the suite on a 16 GB laptop.

Host memory during the run

The 25 GB floor is the idle host (IDE Java language servers, Docker containers), not the suite. Headroom above peak: 9 GB.

Every curve flattens by about forkCount 4. On the loom/**-only strategy, 1 → 4 is worth 6.0 minutes; 4 → 16 adds only 85 more seconds. That is Amdahl's law on this suite: past a handful of forks each module's makespan is pinned by its own slowest single class, and WhisperNodeTest's 15m 04s is a floor that no amount of forking moves.

Note the difference in the last columns: the biggest single number in this table is not produced by forkCount at all. Removing the three heavy ML classes from mvn test takes the suite from 25m 55s to 10m 10s at forkCount=1 — before any fork change.

The model is optimistic: it assumes forks do not contend. In reality they share 24 cores, one Postgres instance and a test-database pool capped at 60 (TESTDATABASE_PROVIDER_POOL_MAXIMUM). §7 measures the gap.

7. Measured validation

The table above is a model, so forkCount was measured directly. The experiment is a back-to-back pair over the loom subtree (mvn -o test -f loom/pom.xml) — the only place where -Dsurefire.forkcount actually applies, and where the heap is capped so memory is not a confound. Same scope, same host, only the fork count changed.

MetricforkCount=1 forkCount=4Change
Wall clock8m 01s 3m 09s -61% (2.5× faster)
Sum of per-fork JVM time7m 54s 11m 39s +48%
Test classes / tests227 / 1,830 227 / 1,830identical
Worst fork RSS494 MB 508 MB +3%
Host memory peak29.6 GB 31.3 GB +1.7 GB
Failures + errors10 233 ×23

Speed: the win is real and larger than modelled. 8m 01s → 3m 09s, a 2.5× speed-up, for +1.7 GB of host memory. The sum of per-fork JVM time rises +48% while wall clock falls — the expected signature of concurrency: each fork is slower because they share cores, but the module finishes far sooner.

Blocker The tests are not isolated for concurrency

At forkCount=1, 10 of 1,830 tests fail. At forkCount=4, 233 fail — on identical code and an identical test set. The suite gets 2.5× faster and simultaneously stops being trustworthy.

It is one root cause, and the test code already documents it. Every test JVM builds its Loom component from the same module-level config directory, and deletes and regenerates the shared JWT keystore inside it:

// loom/core/src/test/java/io/metaloom/loom/core/LoomCoreTestExtension.java:85
// TODO use tempfile to avoid collisions
File baseFolder = new File("target", "test-config");
File keystoreFile = new File(baseFolder, "keystore.jceks");
if (keystoreFile.exists()) {
    keystoreFile.delete();
}

With one fork this is serialised and safe. With four, one JVM deletes or half-writes the keystore while another reads it, and the read fails inside AuthModule.jwtAuthProvider:

java.lang.RuntimeException: java.io.IOException: Tag number over 30 is not supported
    at io.vertx.ext.auth.jwt.impl.JWTAuthProviderImpl.<init>(JWTAuthProviderImpl.java:121)
    at io.metaloom.loom.auth.jwt.AuthModule.jwtAuthProvider(AuthModule.java:54)

That signature — a truncated keystore — accounts for the large majority of the new failures, and 66 of the affected classes are in loom/core. This is a test-infrastructure defect, not a product defect, and it is the gate on the 2.5×. Give each fork its own config directory (Files.createTempDirectory, or target/test-config-${surefire.forkNumber}) and re-run this experiment before changing the default.

Scope note: this pair covers the loom subtree only (227 classes, 1,830 tests) — that is deliberate, because surefire.forkcount has no effect elsewhere. A whole-reactor run at forkCount=4 was also attempted but aborted when a cortex fork failed to start (exit code 250) under memory pressure — itself a demonstration of the uncapped-heap problem in §5.

8. Recommendations

In priority order — by value delivered per unit of risk.

1. Move WhisperNodeTest out of mvn test biggest win, lowest risk

This is one class. It is 65% of all test time on its own, because four of its methods each run a real Whisper transcription:

  • WhisperNodeTest — 15m 04s (11 tests, 64.8% of test time) in cortex/nodes/whisper/core
  • also ML-backed, far smaller: CaptioningNodeTest — 9.5s (8 tests, 0.7% of test time) in cortex/nodes/captioning/core
  • also ML-backed, far smaller: SceneDetectionNodeTest — 8.3s (9 tests, 0.6% of test time) in cortex/nodes/scene-detection/core

The other two are the same category and worth moving with it, but be clear about the arithmetic: WhisperNodeTest is the entire effect.

Rename them to *IT so failsafe owns them, or tag them with a JUnit @Tag excluded by default — loom/pom.xml already threads ${surefire.excludedGroups} through for exactly this purpose, and the root configuration would need the same. Expected: 25m 55s → 10m 10s with no other change and no loss of coverage (they still run, in the phase built for them). A developer's inner loop should not wait on Whisper transcribing a speech four times.

2. Put a heap ceiling on the root/cortex surefire configuration prerequisite for any global fork change

Add an explicit <argLine> to the root pom.xml's surefire configuration — start at something like -Xmx2g and raise it per-module only where a test genuinely needs it. Today a single fork can reach 27.8 GB simply because nothing stops it. This is worth doing on its own, independent of forkCount: it is what makes the suite's memory behaviour predictable on smaller machines.

3. Give each fork its own config directory, then raise forkCount to 4 order matters

These two are one change, and the order is not optional. §7 measured forkCount=4 on loom/** as 8m 01s → 3m 09s with essentially no extra memory — and with failures rising from 10 to 233, because every fork shares target/test-config and races on the JWT keystore in it.

  1. Fix LoomCoreTestExtension (line 85, which already says // TODO use tempfile to avoid collisions) to allocate a per-fork directory — Files.createTempDirectory, or target/test-config-${surefire.forkNumber}, which surefire substitutes per fork. Audit the other fixtures for the same pattern.
  2. Re-run the §7 experiment and confirm the failure count returns to baseline.
  3. Only then change the surefire.forkcount default from 1 to 4 in loom/pom.xml and loom-shared/pom.xml. Those modules are capped at -Xmx256m and peak at 502 MB per fork, so four is under 2 GB.

Do not go much past 4–6: the model flattens there, and the shared Postgres instance and the 60-database test pool become the next constraint.

4. Review reuseForks=false for loom/** needs an isolation review

238 JVM starts cost about 2m 00s across the run. With 361 of 502 test classes finishing in under a second, most of those JVMs spend more time starting than testing. But reuseForks=false is a real isolation guarantee, so this is not a free switch — it needs a check that these tests do not leak static state, Vert.x instances, Dagger components or system properties across classes. Worth the review precisely because it is the largest remaining structural saving.

5. Only then consider a parallel reactor

mvn -T 1C test attacks the Maven-side portion instead of the test-side one. On this warm build that portion was only 15.9s, so it is near-worthless here — but on a clean build, where compilation dominates, it is the main lever. It multiplies peak memory, so it depends on (2).

Explicitly not recommended

  • A global forkCount increase — unsafe until (2) lands; 27.8 GB × N does not fit.
  • forkCount above ~6 — the modelled curve is flat past 4, and the test-database pool (max 60) and the single Postgres instance become the binding constraint.
  • JUnit method-level parallelism — tests allocate a database per test method; intra-class concurrency would need a much larger pool and a full isolation review first.
  • Chasing the 17 failing tests as a performance item — they are pre-existing correctness issues (see §10), unrelated to timing.

10. Method and caveats

  • Per-test timings come from surefire's own XML reports (target/surefire-reports/TEST-*.xml). They measure the test body and exclude JVM startup.
  • Per-fork wall time and peak memory come from replacing surefire's jvm with a wrapper that execs the real JDK and then reports getrusage(RUSAGE_CHILDREN).ru_maxrss — the kernel's own high-water mark, not a sampled estimate. Measured wrapper cost: 15 ms per fork, about 4s across the run (0.3% of wall clock).
  • Fork → class attribution matches fork exit times against surefire report file mtimes within each module. Where one fork covers many classes, its peak is reported for each of them and labelled as shared rather than being split.
  • The host was not quiet. An IDE with several Java language servers and Docker containers ran throughout — that is the 25 GB memory floor and some CPU. Absolute wall times would be lower on a dedicated machine; the ratios, the memory peaks and the comparison between the two runs are unaffected.
  • This was a warm build. Sources were already compiled, so Maven-side cost is only 15.9s. On a clean build that share is much larger, and forkCount does not touch it.
  • 17 tests do not pass at this revision. They ran with -Dmaven.test.failure.ignore=true so the whole reactor would execute. They are pre-existing correctness issues unrelated to performance — but note that a class which errors early is faster here than it would be when passing, so those rows understate their true cost. The two clusters are loom-client/rest (LoomContainer is registered with @RegisterExtension but does not implement JUnit's Extension) and loom-service-auth-jwt (VertxPermTest NPEs on a null basePath).
  • The scheduling model in §6 assumes independent forks. They share CPU, one Postgres instance and a 60-database pool, so treat modelled figures as an upper bound — §7 measures the real gap.
  • Out of scope: e2e-test (Playwright, needs a running server) and all failsafe *IT tests, which mvn test does not execute.
